0.name: Mafeking Old Hands
0.text:
The Mafeking Old Hands are the British expatriate officials who ran the Bechuanaland Protectorate from Mafeking, across the border in South Africa, until the capital moved to Gaborone in 1965. Many stayed on after independence in 1966 as permanent secretaries, district commissioners, police officers and advisers.

They favour firm administration, close ties with Britain and the Commonwealth and caution toward the liberation movements operating near the borders. Suspicious of rapid localisation and of party politics, they prize order and efficiency. Their leverage lies in their grip on the civil service, the police and development planning, for Botswana still lacks enough trained citizens to replace them.

1.name: Botswana Democratic Party
1.text:
The Botswana Democratic Party was founded in 1962 by Seretse Khama, heir to the Bangwato chieftaincy, with Quett Masire and others. It won independence in 1966 and was re-elected in October 1969 with 24 of 31 seats, although Masire lost his own seat to the former Bangwaketse chief Bathoen II.

The BDP stands for non-racial democracy, cautious development, the rule of law and good relations with both the West and its white-ruled neighbours, while refusing to recognise apartheid. It looks to the new diamond finds at Orapa to finance roads, schools and water. Its base lies among cattle owners, rural voters and the Bangwato heartland.

2.name: Botswana Independence Party
2.text:
The Botswana Independence Party was founded in 1964 by Motsamai Mpho after a split in the Botswana People's Party. It holds a single seat after the 1969 election, won by Mpho in the north-west, where the party has its strongest base among the Bayei and other minorities around Maun and Ngamiland.

The BIP calls for faster localisation of the civil service, development of neglected regions and the protection of minority communities against Tswana dominance. It is moderate in tone and non-aligned, though friendly to the West. Its leverage is small but real in the north-west, and its single member can bargain with the government on regional demands.

3.name: Botswana National Front
3.text:
The Botswana National Front was founded in 1965 by Kenneth Koma, a Marxist intellectual educated abroad, as a broad front against the BDP. In 1969 it won three seats after recruiting Bathoen II, who abdicated as chief of the Bangwaketse to stand for parliament and defeated Vice-President Quett Masire in Kanye.

The BNF calls for socialism, national control of mineral wealth, land reform and solidarity with the liberation movements in southern Africa. It combines urban workers, teachers and students with the conservative Bangwaketse following of Bathoen. Its leverage lies in being the main voice of opposition, though the uneasy alliance between Marxists and traditionalists strains it.

4.name: Kgotla ya Babereki
4.text:
Kgotla ya Babereki, the workers' assembly, is a small Marxist-Leninist cadre group within the orbit of the Botswana National Front. Its members are teachers, clerks and returned students who absorbed Kenneth Koma's teaching and studied pamphlets from Moscow and Prague.

The group wants a vanguard party, the nationalisation of the mines and cattle ranches, and alignment with the Soviet bloc and the ANC and ZAPU exiles. It condemns the BDP as a party of chiefs and cattle barons serving Western capital. Its numbers are tiny, but it supplies much of the ideological energy of the left and has contacts in Lusaka and Dar es Salaam.

5.name: Botswana People's Party
5.text:
The Botswana People's Party was founded in 1960 as the first nationalist party in the protectorate, inspired by the ANC and PAC of South Africa. Led by Philip Matante, it won three seats in 1969, all in the north-east around Francistown, where it is strongest among workers and the Kalanga.

The BPP demands radical Pan-Africanism, rapid localisation, an end to dependence on South Africa and support for the armed liberation struggle. It is hostile to the West and to the expatriate presence and suspicious of chiefly power. Its leverage lies in the Francistown townships and among labour migrants, though repeated splits have weakened it.

6.name: Batho ba ga Bathoen
6.text:
Batho ba ga Bathoen, Bathoen's people, are the loyal following of Bathoen II, the former kgosi of the Bangwaketse, who abdicated in 1969 to fight the BDP from within the Botswana National Front. Centred on Kanye, they swept the Ngwaketse constituencies in October 1969.

They oppose the Chieftainship Act and the BDP's transfer of land and power from the dikgosi to elected councils and the central government. Deeply conservative, they ally with the socialist left only out of hostility to Seretse Khama's modernising state and to Western-style centralisation. Their leverage lies in the loyalty of the Bangwaketse and the prestige of the chieftaincy.

7.name: Special Branch
7.text:
The Special Branch of the Botswana Police is the country's small intelligence and security service, inherited from the protectorate administration. It watches refugees and liberation movement members passing through Francistown and Lobatse, and the agents South Africa and Rhodesia send to follow them.

Its officers favour surveillance, deportation and quiet pressure over open politics, and some would like sweeping emergency powers to guard against cross-border raids and subversion. It distrusts all foreign influence, Western and Eastern alike. Its leverage lies in its files on exiles and opposition figures and in its role as the government's eyes on the frontier.

8.name: Khoja Jamaat
8.text:
The Khoja Jamaat is a handful of Shia trading families of Gujarati origin in Francistown and Lobatse, linked by kinship to the larger Khoja communities of East Africa and Rhodesia. They meet for prayer and Muharram gatherings in private homes and shops.

The community values education, commerce and good relations with the government, which treats Asian traders more fairly than its neighbours do. It keeps out of politics and supports Botswana's non-racial constitution. Its influence is limited to its members and their business networks, which reach across southern and eastern Africa.

9.name: Hussaini Majlis
9.text:
The Hussaini Majlis is a small devotional gathering of young Shia men in Francistown who host visiting preachers from East Africa and read the writings of clerics trained in Najaf. They organise the Muharram mourning rituals for the community.

They call for strict observance and obedience to the senior Shia clergy, and see Western secular culture as a corruption of faith. They have no political organisation and only a few followers, but they follow the activist clerics of Iraq and Iran closely and could carry revolutionary religious ideas into a community that has so far been purely commercial.

10.name: Tablighi Jamaat
10.text:
The Tablighi Jamaat, the missionary movement founded in India in 1926, reaches Botswana through the Gujarati Muslim traders of Lobatse, Gaborone and Francistown and through preaching parties from South Africa. Its members travel between the small mosques and trading stores along the railway line.

The movement rejects politics and calls Muslims to prayer, piety and correct conduct. It accepts the authorities, preaches obedience and avoids any confrontation. Its influence lies in its network of traders and mosques, which makes it the most organised Islamic body in a country where Muslims are a small minority.

11.name: Dar al-Hijra
11.text:
Dar al-Hijra is a tiny circle of young Muslims in Lobatse and Gaborone, sons of traders who studied in Pakistan or the Arab world and returned with pamphlets on the caliphate. They meet in private and correspond with like-minded groups in South Africa.

They reject secular nationalism, Western democracy and Soviet communism alike, and dream of a single Islamic state uniting the Muslim world. They have no arms, no public presence and only a few members, and they are known to the police mainly as a curiosity among the Asian merchant community.

12.name: Ummah Study Circle
12.text:
The Ummah Study Circle gathers educated Muslims in Gaborone and Lobatse, teachers, clerks and traders of Asian and Malawian origin, who read the works of Hasan al-Banna and Abul A'la Maududi. It is inspired by Muslim youth groups in Cape Town and Durban.

The circle wants Muslims to take part in public life, build schools and welfare bodies and work with Christians for justice. It praises Botswana's non-racial constitution and condemns apartheid across the border as contrary to Islam. Its influence is limited to education and charity, but it gives young Muslims a voice in the new capital.

13.name: The Gaborone Secretariat
13.text:
The Gaborone Secretariat is the small, powerful core of planners and permanent secretaries in the Office of the President and the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning. Working under Vice-President Quett Masire, they drew up the first National Development Plan and negotiated the 1969 diamond agreement with De Beers.

They favour centralised planning, fiscal discipline and careful use of mineral revenue, keeping politics at arm's length from development. They are neither pro-Western nor pro-Eastern but pragmatic, seeking aid from all sides. Their leverage lies in controlling budgets and mineral negotiations, which makes them indispensable to any government.

14.name: Ntlo ya Dikgosi
14.text:
The House of Chiefs was created by the independence constitution of 1966 as an advisory chamber of the principal dikgosi of the eight major Tswana merafe, together with elected sub-chiefs. It must be consulted on bills affecting custom, tribal land and the chieftaincy.

The chiefs defend customary law, the kgotla and their role in land allocation, and resent the BDP's laws that transferred tribal land and revenue to land boards and councils. They are conservative, non-aligned and suspicious of party politics. Their leverage lies in their authority over rural communities and in Seretse Khama's own status as heir to the Bangwato chieftaincy.

15.name: De Beers Botswana Mining Company
15.text:
The De Beers Botswana Mining Company was formed in 1969 by De Beers and the government to develop the diamond pipe discovered at Orapa in 1967. Harry Oppenheimer's group holds the controlling share, and the mine is due to begin production in 1971.

The company stands for foreign investment, stable taxation and close cooperation with the state, and its diamonds promise to transform one of the world's poorest countries. It is tied to South African and Western capital through the Anglo American empire. Its leverage lies in the revenues the government is counting on to finance its development plans.

16.name: Francistown Traders
16.text:
The Francistown Traders are the white, Asian and Motswana merchants of Botswana's main commercial town, whose shops, butcheries and transport firms serve the north-east and the cattle trade with Rhodesia. Many have been in business since the protectorate era.

They want free enterprise, low taxes, open borders for trade with Rhodesia and South Africa and fewer licensing rules, and they distrust state trading schemes and the radical opposition. They are pragmatic and pro-Western. Their leverage lies in their control of the retail trade and credit in the north and in their contacts with BDP ministers.

17.name: Okavango Guardians
17.text:
The Okavango Guardians are the wildlife officers, safari operators, researchers and Maun residents who campaign to protect the Okavango Delta, the Chobe National Park created in 1967 and the Central Kalahari reserve. They fear the plans to drain the delta's waters for mining and irrigation.

They call for protected areas, controls on hunting and veterinary fences, and respect for the San who live in the Kalahari. They avoid party politics and look to Western conservation bodies for support. Their leverage lies in international attention and the hope that tourism can become a second pillar of the economy.

18.name: Brigades Movement
18.text:
The Brigades Movement grew out of Swaneng Hill School in Serowe, founded in 1963 by the South African exile Patrick van Rensburg. Its builders', farmers' and textile brigades train school-leavers in practical skills while their work pays for their education.

The movement promotes self-reliance, education with production, cooperatives and equality, and rejects both the colonial elite school model and Western-style consumerism. It is non-aligned and inspired by Nyerere's African socialism. Its leverage lies in youth, rural communities and international volunteers, and its model is spreading to other villages across Botswana.

19.name: Ba ga Mao
19.text:
Ba ga Mao, Mao's people, are a small group of radical students and young teachers who discovered the Little Red Book at the University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland in Roma and in the secondary schools. Some have links with PAC exiles inspired by Beijing.

They call for a peasant revolution, collective farms, the expropriation of the cattle barons and an end to dependence on South Africa and the West. They reject the Soviet Union as revisionist and the BNF leadership as too cautious. They have little organisation, but they agitate in schools and student bodies.

20.name: Botswana ke ya Batswana
20.text:
Botswana ke ya Batswana, Botswana belongs to the Batswana, is the rallying cry of young civil servants, traders and unemployed school-leavers who resent the expatriates and immigrants holding the best jobs and businesses. It finds echoes on the BDP backbenches as well as in the opposition.

Its supporters demand rapid localisation of the civil service, licences reserved for citizens and restrictions on foreign traders. They are suspicious of refugees from Rhodesia and South Africa, whom they see as competitors and security risks. Their leverage lies in popular resentment and the pressure it puts on the government to speed up localisation.

21.name: Ghanzi Boere
21.text:
The Ghanzi Boere are Afrikaner ranching families of the Ghanzi freehold block in western Botswana, descendants of settlers brought in by Cecil Rhodes in the 1890s. Isolated in the Kalahari, they look to South Africa for markets, schooling and politics.

Many reject the non-racial republic, resent black officials and dream of union with South Africa or white control of the west. They admire apartheid and the National Party, and some keep close ties with the South African security services. Their numbers are small, but their land and frontier position make them a potential fifth column.

22.name: Police Mobile Unit
22.text:
The Police Mobile Unit is the paramilitary arm of the Botswana Police and the country's only armed force, since Botswana has chosen not to raise an army. Its few hundred men patrol the long borders with Rhodesia, South Africa and South West Africa.

Its officers are professional and loyal to the government, though they are acutely aware of the danger of cross-border raids and guerrilla movements in the region. They argue for better equipment and the creation of a proper defence force. Their leverage lies in being the only body able to defend the frontier and in the government's growing anxiety about border security.

23.name: Bogosi jwa Bangwato
23.text:
The Bangwato royal house descends from Khama III, the Christian king who secured British protection in 1885 and ruled from Serowe. Seretse Khama is its heir, but he renounced the chieftaincy in 1956 after his exile over his marriage to Ruth Williams, and his young son Ian is seen as the future kgosi.

Royalists want the dignity and authority of the dikgosi restored and the Bangwato kingdom respected within the republic. They are conservative and deeply attached to Serowe and the kgotla. Their leverage lies in Seretse's double role as royal heir and president, which keeps the largest merafe loyal to the BDP.
